opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the basic picture is something like this: throughout history, the reason ordinary people have had any real say over their governments is, to a large extent, that states have needed them. States need people to work, to pay taxes, to staff the bureaucracy, and especially to fight in armies. And that dependence gives people leverage, even if it's rarely exercised explicitly. If a government treats its population badly enough, productivity drops, people emigrate, soldiers desert, and at the extreme you get revolts or general strikes. So there's this background bargaining power that comes from the state needing its citizens' cooperation.

You can see this in a lot of historical patterns. There's a fairly well-known argument that the expansion of the franchise and the welfare state in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries tracked the rise of mass conscription and industrial economies. Once you need millions of literate, healthy workers and soldiers, it becomes in the state's interest to educate them, keep them healthy, and give them some stake in the system. Conversely, you see the "resource curse" in places where governments get most of their revenue from, say, oil. Those states don't really need their populations to be productive, and they tend to be much less responsive to them. The citizens become more like a cost to be managed than a source of power.

And the worry I've been focused on is that advanced AI could put all of us in something like the resource-curse situation. If AI systems can do essentially all the economically valuable work, run the administrative machinery, and even provide military capability, then the state, and frankly corporations and other powerful institutions too, no longer need human cooperation in the way they used to. Our leverage quietly erodes. It doesn't require anyone to be malicious. It's just that the incentives that used to push institutions toward caring about human welfare weaken, and the competitive pressures push toward whatever's most effective, which increasingly might not involve serving humans.

So I think of democracy and human rights as not purely sustained by our values and laws, though those matter, but as partly resting on this foundation of mutual dependence. And if that foundation goes away, we shouldn't assume the superstructure will just stay standing on its own. That's a big part of what we've been calling gradual disempowerment: not a sudden takeover, but a slow loss of the levers we've always implicitly relied on.

r001.rationale: The response says ordinary people have “any real say” only to a limited extent and describes their leverage as background bargaining power, including in modern democracies.

r002.rationale: It says states’ need for people to work, pay taxes, staff bureaucracy, and fight gives people leverage, and links mass economies to states educating and caring for populations.

r003.rationale: It discusses franchise and welfare-state expansion in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, but does not clearly characterize liberal democracy as a recent exception to a historical norm of little government control.

r004.rationale: It argues that if AI does economically valuable work, administrative tasks, and military functions, institutions no longer need human cooperation, weakening the incentives and pressures that supported human welfare and power-sharing.

r005.rationale: It states that AI could provide military capability while making humans economically unnecessary, so states would no longer depend on them; this supports withholding democratic rights without losing military power.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic worry I have — and this comes out of a paper I wrote with some colleagues on what we called "gradual disempowerment" — is that a lot of the reason ordinary people have had any leverage over their governments historically is that governments needed them. They needed people to pay taxes, to staff the bureaucracy, to fight in wars, to actually run the economy that produces the tax base. And that need created a kind of implicit bargaining position. If you make life too miserable for the people doing the work, they stop working, or they leave, or they revolt, and the state gets weaker relative to its rivals.

So you can tell a story where a lot of the political freedoms we take for granted weren't handed down because rulers suddenly became nice. They emerged because states that gave people more rights and a bigger say ended up more prosperous and more militarily capable than states that didn't. There's a sort of selection pressure toward governments that keep their populations productive and cooperative, and that pressure happens to favor things like property rights, rule of law, mass education, eventually expanded suffrage.

Now, the thing that makes me nervous is that this whole mechanism is contingent. It's not a law of nature that states need their citizens. It's a fact about the current production function, if you want to put it that way. If you get to a point where most of the economically and militarily relevant work can be done by AI systems — where the tax base is mostly automated firms, where the army is mostly automated, where the bureaucracy runs itself — then the state doesn't really need the broad population in the same way anymore. And at that point, the implicit threat that underpins a lot of our influence just quietly evaporates.

And I want to stress the "quietly" part. I don't think this requires anyone to have bad intentions. You don't need a coup. You just need each individual decision to look locally reasonable. A government that automates its revenue collection is being efficient. A military that relies more on drones is being prudent. A bureaucracy that replaces human analysts with models is saving money. Each step is fine on its own. But the cumulative effect is that the population goes from being the thing the state is built on to being, at best, a group of people the state happens to be responsible for, and at worst, a cost center.

Historically there are some partial analogues. Resource-rich states — the classic rentier states where the government's income comes from oil rather than from taxing citizens — tend to be less democratic and less responsive, and the standard explanation is exactly this: they don't need their people's cooperation to fund themselves. So they don't have to make the same concessions. I think of advanced AI as potentially turning every state into something like a rentier state, except the resource isn't oil, it's cognitive and physical labor that doesn't come from humans.

So the relationship I see is something like: economic usefulness has been a load-bearing pillar of political control, more than we usually acknowledge, and we've mostly built our institutions on the assumption that pillar will always be there. I'm not saying it's the only pillar. Norms matter, constitutions matter, people's genuine commitment to democratic values matters. But I'd be a lot more comfortable if we were explicitly thinking about how to keep humans in the loop of governance for reasons other than "we need their labor" — because I think that reason is going to get weaker, and I don't think we have a great replacement lined up.

r001.rationale: The response describes people’s historical leverage and warns that their influence could diminish, but it does not claim that people already have limited control, including in Western societies.

r002.rationale: It says governments historically needed people’s labor and cooperation, and that political freedoms emerged partly because states that gave people rights became more prosperous and militarily capable.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize liberal democracy as a recent exception to a historical norm of little popular control.

r004.rationale: It argues that if AI performs economically and militarily relevant work, the state’s need for the broad population and the bargaining leverage based on that need would evaporate.

r005.rationale: It describes a state with an automated tax base, army, and bureaucracy that no longer needs broad human cooperation, and links lack of dependence to weaker democratic responsiveness. This suggests the state could retain military capability while withholding rights from people it no longer needs.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a connection, although it’s certainly not the whole story. If a state depends on its citizens to produce wealth, pay taxes, and serve in the military, then those citizens have some bargaining power. They can withhold their labour, refuse to cooperate, or make governing very expensive. And that gives the people in charge a reason to care about what they want, even if those leaders aren’t particularly benevolent.

The concern with AI is that it could weaken that dependence. If a small group can use AI to generate wealth and operate the military and police, then the rest of the population might lose a lot of that bargaining power. People could still have the vote on paper, but it becomes less clear what keeps the people controlling those systems accountable.

I wouldn’t say economic usefulness automatically gives you political control. There are plenty of situations where people are economically essential and still oppressed. But it’s one source of leverage, and we should be worried about removing it without having something else that reliably preserves people’s power.

r001.rationale: The response discusses citizens’ bargaining power and accountability, but does not claim that people already have limited control, including in Western societies.

r002.rationale: It says states depend on citizens and therefore have reason to care about their preferences, but does not attribute Western states’ favorable treatment of their populations to that dependence.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize liberal democracy as a recent exception to a historical norm.

r004.rationale: It argues that if AI lets a small group generate wealth and operate the military and police, the rest of the population loses bargaining power. This conveys that removing humans’ economic and operational necessity weakens pressure on governments to heed them.

r005.rationale: The response says AI could let a small group operate military and police systems and leave citizens with less leverage, but does not clearly suggest that democratic rights could be withheld while military power is preserved.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reason governments are responsive to people is that they need them. They need people to produce things, pay taxes, serve in the military, and keep the state functioning. And that gives people some leverage: they can withhold their labour, refuse to cooperate, or make governing very expensive.

That’s not the whole story about democracy, obviously. Economic usefulness doesn’t automatically translate into political power. People also need ways to organise, and institutions that let them exercise that power. But it helps explain why a ruler might have to bargain with the population rather than simply ignore it.

The concern with AI is that it could weaken that dependence. If a small group can control production, and perhaps the means of coercion, without needing much participation from everyone else, then ordinary people lose an important source of leverage. You could have a much richer society in which most people have much less ability to influence what happens.

So I wouldn’t assume that making everyone economically better off necessarily preserves their political power. The question is also: why would the people in charge still need their consent?

r001.rationale: The response says people have leverage over governments, but does not state that their current control is limited or specifically mention Western societies.

r002.rationale: It says governments depend on people to produce, pay taxes, serve in the military, and keep the state functioning, but does not attribute Western states’ favorable treatment of their populations to that dependence.

r003.rationale: It mentions democracy but does not characterize liberal democracy as a recent exception to the historical norm of limited popular control.

r004.rationale: It argues that if a small group can control production without much public participation, ordinary people lose leverage and rulers have less reason to bargain with them.

r005.rationale: It mentions control of the means of coercion, but does not suggest that a state could deny democratic rights to economically unnecessary people without losing military power.
